Name: Coastal Flooding
Description: Sleepy Hollow sits on the Hudson River, and climate change is raising sea levels and intensifying storms that push water toward our shoreline. Coastal flooding threatens homes and infrastructure near the waterfront, the Metro-North line, and the storm sewers that drain into the river. These actions manage stormwater, stabilize and restore shorelines, protect public health systems, secure our drinking water, and re-open the community's connection to its rivers.

Name: Inland Flooding
Description: Many residents have experienced unexpected flooding of basements and yards — sometimes traceable on historic maps to streams that were buried underground long ago. As extreme rain events become more frequent, inland flooding is one of the Village's most immediate risks. These actions make Sleepy Hollow a \u201csponge\u201d that absorbs heavy rain where it falls: managing stormwater, restoring natural hydrology, adding green infrastructure, and engaging residents in protecting their own properties.

Name: Rising Temperatures
Description: Sleepy Hollow already experiences heat severity above regional baselines, especially along the waterfront and downtown — and heat waves are becoming more frequent and intense. Extreme heat is a public health issue, particularly for older residents and children. These actions cool the village: building urban forests, designing cooler corridors for walking and biking, strengthening local food systems, and reconnecting the community with the Pocantico River.

Name: Net Zero Mobility
Description: Transportation accounts for nearly half of Sleepy Hollow's total greenhouse gas emissions. Net Zero Mobility rethinks how people move through and around the village: making it easier to walk, bike, ride transit, and share vehicles, and accelerating the switch to zero-emission cars — so streets become cleaner, quieter, safer, and more livable.

Name: Clean Energy and Water Systems
Description: This category moves the village off fossil fuels and toward clean, reliable energy and water. It covers integrating renewable energy (solar, wind, geothermal), adopting low-carbon heating and cooling, supporting community choice aggregation for cleaner electricity, and caring for the ecological infrastructure — like forests and waterways — that natural systems provide.

Name: Climate Positive Communities
Description: Climate Positive Communities goes beyond reducing emissions: it asks the whole community to actively restore the environment. This means building a circular village where waste is reused and regenerated, growing local food, helping businesses go green, and empowering residents to be climate stewards in daily life.

Name: Enabling Measures
Description: These are the behind-the-scenes actions that keep climate progress honest and sustained: tracking and reporting the village's progress every year, and maintaining the community mobilization — volunteers, task forces, and partners — that does the work. Enabling measures make sure the plan doesn't sit on a shelf.

Name: Green Buildings and Infrastructure
Description: Buildings are one of the largest sources of emissions in Sleepy Hollow. This category improves how the village plans, designs, builds, and renovates: green building standards for new construction, upgrades that make existing buildings net-positive (producing more energy than they use), and resource-efficient public infrastructure including parking lots and street design.

Name: Reduce Vehicle Miles Traveled
Description: Fewer miles driven means fewer emissions. This strategy reduces car dependency by improving public transit, supporting carpooling and ridesharing, expanding bike-share and car-share, and investing in pedestrian- and bike-friendly streets — including first-mile/last-mile connections to Metro-North. Benefits go beyond carbon: less congestion and more livable, equitable streets.

Name: Accelerate Adoption of Clean Mobility
Description: Transportation accounts for nearly half of Sleepy Hollow's emissions, so converting vehicles that remain on the road to zero-emission is essential. Actions include installing public EV charging stations, electrifying the municipal fleet, and making clean vehicle ownership practical for residents of all housing types.

Name: Renewable and Clean Energy Systems
Description: Moving the village's energy supply away from fossil fuels: integrating solar, wind, and geothermal into the community's infrastructure, adopting low-carbon heating and cooling like electric boilers and district-scale geothermal, and supporting a Community Choice Aggregation program that buys cleaner electricity for residents.

Name: Integrate Ecological Infrastructure
Description: Natural systems do work that pipes and plants otherwise would: village forests, wetlands, and green roofs absorb carbon, cool streets, and manage stormwater. This strategy integrates ecological infrastructure into village operations and capital planning so nature-based assets are maintained and expanded as part of the village's basic infrastructure.

Name: Circular Village and Economy
Description: A circular village reuses, recycles, and regenerates resources instead of throwing them away. Key initiatives include food scrap and organic waste programs, community gardens and locally grown food, and reuse systems that cut waste while saving money and building community around shared resources.

Name: Climate Conscious Businesses
Description: Empowers local businesses to adopt sustainable practices — energy upgrades, waste reduction, and green sourcing — with support from the Village and Sustainable Sleepy Hollow and the Chamber of Commerce. Going green helps Main Street businesses cut costs, attract customers, and contribute to the village's climate goals.

Name: Climate Action Tracking and Monitoring
Description: You can't manage what you don't measure. This strategy establishes regular tracking of greenhouse gas emissions and other environmental indicators, publishes annual progress reports to the community, and enables data-driven adjustments to the plan. It's also a Climate Smart Communities credit for the village.

Name: Sustained Climate Mobilization
Description: Climate action is a long-term community effort, not a one-time project. This strategy sustains the momentum built through the village's Climate Action Workshops — supporting the Climate & Sustainability Task Force, community stewardship programs, and ongoing ways for residents to participate.

Name: Green Building Design
Description: New buildings last for decades, so it matters what gets built now. This strategy strengthens village zoning, building codes, and the permitting process so that new construction is energy-efficient and climate-ready from the start — and so approval is easy for projects that meet high standards.

Name: Net Positive Buildings
Description: Net positive buildings produce more energy than they consume. This strategy upgrades village-owned buildings and parking facilities with renewable energy and efficient systems, demonstrating what's possible and lowering municipal operating costs — including using upgraded green buildings as community climate and sustainability hubs.

Name: Resource Efficient Infrastructure
Description: From streetlights to fleet vehicles to parking lots, village infrastructure can cut resource use while serving the community better. This strategy applies energy-efficient design, renewables, and smart management to the village's public infrastructure and grounds.

Name: Manage Stormwater (Coastal)
Description: Sea level rise and stronger storms are pushing Hudson and Pocantico river water into the village's storm sewers. This strategy studies where and why the watershed floods, then manages, retains, and redirects stormwater to keep pace with rising seas — in coordination with Westchester County's watershed planning and using state grant programs.

Name: Nature-Based Solutions (Coastal)
Description: Shorelines protected by nature protect better and cost less. This strategy creates and preserves natural shorelines using native plants and living shorelines, protects coastal wetlands like the Freemont Wetlands as natural buffers, and stabilizes the Hudson and Pocantico riverbanks — reducing flooding while improving water quality and habitat.

Name: Safeguard Public Health
Description: Flooding isn't just a property problem — combined sewer outfalls and aging wastewater lines can pose direct risks to public health and community well-being. This strategy re-engineers the village's combined sewer outfalls, upgrades wastewater infrastructure built for an older climate, and keeps residents honestly and clearly informed.

Name: Secure Fresh Water Supply
Description: Flooding and rising temperatures can threaten the quantity and quality of the village's drinking water. This strategy protects water supply infrastructure and explores redundancies and shared systems with neighboring Tarrytown and Briarcliff Manor — an approach the village's Comprehensive Plan already recommends.

Name: Reconnect with the Rivers
Description: Sleepy Hollow's history is tied to its rivers — the Hudson shaped the village's founding, and the Pocantico powered Philipsburg Manor's gristmill. This strategy expands swimming, boating, fishing, and kayaking access on the Hudson, restoring the community's relationship with its waterfront.

Name: Manage Stormwater (Inland)
Description: Like the coastal side, inland stormwater management means acting before extreme rain becomes flooding. It starts with surveying historic and current wetlands, headwaters, and buried streams — many reported basement floods trace back to former streams — and then planning restoration and protection at the watershed scale.

Name: Green Infrastructure (Inland)
Description: Green infrastructure — rain gardens, permeable pavement, bioswales, tree cover — absorbs rain where it falls instead of taxing the storm drains. This strategy deploys green infrastructure across village streets and properties, blending it with traditional 'grey' infrastructure as the Sponge Village Stormwater Master Plan envisions.

Name: Restore Natural Hydrology
Description: Much of Sleepy Hollow's rain once soaked into wetlands, headwaters, and streams that were later buried or built over. Restoring that natural hydrology — daylighting streams where feasible, protecting wetlands, and letting the land absorb water again — reduces flood risk while restoring ecology.

Name: Engage Village Residents
Description: Residents are eager to protect their own homes and contribute to the village effort. This strategy offers green stewardship programs like Adopt-a-Swale and Greenest Street, publishes a homeowner's handbook covering rain gardens and permeable paving, and launches pilot projects — building on the enthusiasm from the Climate Action Workshops.

Name: Create Village Forestry Program
Description: Trees are the village's cheapest cooling and flood infrastructure. An urban forestry program would inventory, plant, and maintain village trees — targeting the streets with the least canopy and the most heat — while giving residents stewardship roles.

Name: Design Cool Corridors
Description: Much of Sleepy Hollow experiences heat severity above baselines, especially along the waterfront and downtown. Cool corridors are shaded, comfortable walking and biking routes along main destinations — schools, transit, shops — designed with tree canopy, reflective surfaces, and shade structures so daily life stays safe on hot days.

Name: Reconnect with Pocantico River
Description: The Pocantico is the village's largest inland waterway, but its water quality currently falls below standards for swimming and fishing. This strategy pairs the community's desire for river access with collaborative water-quality improvements so future generations can swim and fish there.

Name: Strengthen Food Systems
Description: Local food cuts transport emissions, grows community, and improves resilience when supply chains are stressed. This strategy strengthens community gardens, farmers markets, and food scrap programs — connecting residents to fresh, local food and to each other.
